title: It's the Reading, Stupid
author: Fitzy
source: Teaching in the Age of AI, July 10, 2026
summary: A career history teacher argues that the AI era has intensified a crisis in reading that schools were already failing to address. Students who cannot read well are unable to evaluate, understand, or benefit from AI output—they lack the accumulated training corpus to notice sycophantic errors, misjudge tone, or catch embedded worldviews. Drawing on Mortimer Adler's 'How to Read a Book,' the author distinguishes levels of reading and observes that schools stop explicitly teaching reading after basic decoding, leaving students without the annotation, close reading, and analytical skills that difficult texts demand. Curricular experiments with AI-simplified texts and custom GPTs trained on textbook chapters reveal a consistent pattern: each convenience that bypasses reading struggle also bypasses the reading growth that struggle produces. The closing argument is that reading instruction—not writing assessment—should be the most urgent pedagogical conversation in the age of AI, and that the strongest students benefit most from AI precisely because they already read well.
points: Reading fluency and critical reading ability determine whether students can engage meaningfully with AI output—students who cannot read well will find AI harmful rather than helpful, unable to catch its confident errors.
The AI era has created a paradox: the technology most likely to produce fluent but flawed text is also the technology that most rewards the skilled, skeptical reader.

Schools typically stop explicit reading instruction after basic decoding, neglecting higher-order skills—annotation, close reading of complex syntax, distinguishing argument from evidence—that difficult texts demand.
Using AI to simplify a difficult text solves the content problem while bypassing the reading problem; multiplied across a semester, this erodes the very skill the accommodation was meant to support.
The students who benefit most from classroom AI are those who already read and write well—they prompt better and actually read the output critically, widening rather than closing the achievement gap.
quotes: The overlooked issue is that if we actually want students to use AI effectively, either in class or at home, the skill we need to worry most about is not writing. It is reading.

I can tell at a glance whether a Google AI summary is likely to be on target, whether I need to read deeper on the topic, quickly locate a trusted article or source to skim, zero in on the section I need, or whether I should regroup entirely and start a new search.
reading is one of those activities which improves exponentially - the more you read, the better you read, the more you understand, and the better you read and understand, the more you want to read.

A student who does not read will struggle to write well, no matter how many outlines and graphic organizers we hand them. Schools need to spend as much time thinking about teaching reading as we do about writing
I solved the content problem by skipping the reading problem.
I would never want students using AI in place of reading the original, but, just as with AI-assisted writing, the risk of reverting to cognitive offloading was too high.
Deep reading has always been the hardest level to sustain and the easiest to lose
the strongest students got the best results. The ones who already read and wrote well quickly figured out how to improve their prompts and, critically, actually read the output with care.
If I could wave a wand and instantly bestow one proficiency on every student I teach, it would be the ability to read deeply. So many doors open once that muscle is built.
